/.title: Hybrid work-from-home policy experiment (Trip.com, Nature 2024)
/.problem: Can we predict the impact of two work-from-home days?
/.situation: In August 2021 Trip.com let half of 1,612 Airfare and IT employees in Shanghai work from home on Wednesdays and Fridays for six months; the other half stayed in the office. Who was offered was decided by birthday, so the two groups are directly comparable.
/.data_used: The experiment's public replication deposit (Nature 2024): one row per employee with commute, family, tenure, role and manager status, plus the measured outcomes: who quit, the endline survey, performance grades and how often home days were taken.
/.protocol_line: Simulation predictions use employee information from before the policy and assumptions from earlier research. Actual outcomes are used to check accuracy.
/.intro: Simulates the 1,612 employees of Trip.com's 2021 hybrid-work experiment as digital twins over six months: half were offered Wednesdays and Fridays at home, half were not. Each twin decides weekly whether to work from home and whether to stay, from its own commute, family, preferences and team. The prediction is scored against the randomized experiment; the alternatives explore offering hybrid work to everyone and adding an AI assistant for customer replies and analysis.
/.world: 1,612 employees in two divisions over six months (Aug 2021 to Jan 2022). Half were randomly offered two WFH days a week. Every real employee is simulated as a digital twin built from their own covariates; outcomes are attrition, satisfaction, performance and the manager contrast, scored at the population level against the randomized experiment.

narrative.title: Hybrid work at Trip.com: simulation prediction and actual outcome
narrative.subtitle: 1612 employees, six months, two WFH days a week offered to half of them. Simulation from pretreatment inputs and assumptions from earlier research; compared with Bloom, Han & Liang (Nature 2024).
takeaways: The simulation predicts a 2.39 percentage-point reduction in six-month attrition from offering two home days a week. The actual reduction was 2.40 points, comparing the hybrid and office-only groups.

Six-month attrition: the simulation predicts 8.6% for office-only employees and 6.3% for employees offered hybrid work. Actual outcomes were 7.2% and 4.8%, respectively. Both simulated rates are too high.
The simulation predicts work satisfaction increasing by +0.37 points on the 0-10 scale; the actual increase was +0.35. Work-life balance: simulation prediction +0.45, actual outcome +0.54.
The retention gain concentrates among non-managers: prediction -2.8 points for non-managers and -1.1 for managers; the experiment measured -3.3 and +0.2.
For performance grades, the simulation predicts a change of +0.02 points; the actual change was -0.06. Both estimates are small.
Simulated employees used 55% of their eligible WFH days; the experiment recorded 52%.

This is a retrospective comparison with published outcomes. Earlier model choices had already been compared with those results; the close overall impact does not establish accuracy on new companies or policies.
Extending the offer to everyone takes company-wide six-month attrition from 7.5% (the experiment as run, simulated) to 6.1%, about 24 fewer resignations among 1612 employees.

sections.heading: What was simulated
sections.body: 1612 employees of Trip.com's Airfare and IT divisions, rebuilt one by one from the experiment's real pretreatment data (age, gender, tenure, graduate degree, children, commute time, volunteer status, prior performance grade, manager flag) and assigned to the arms exactly as the birthday lottery did: 820 / 792 office-only / offered hybrid work. Each employee works an hourly schedule from 9 Aug 2021 to 23 Jan 2022, performing O*NET-bound activities of their role, commuting on office days and, in the group offered hybrid work, deciding every Wednesday and Friday whether to work from home. Latent commute burden, work-life balance, job satisfaction and attachment update weekly; a weekly quit hazard turns those states into resignations. The endline survey (21 Jan 2022) and the 2021H2 performance review are simulated as the company recorded them. The prediction was run over 50 seeds with every behavioral parameter drawn from its prior range, so the intervals reflect prior uncertainty and simulated outcome variation. This is a retrospective evaluation, not an untouched prospective test.

sections.heading: Before the policy and the other predictions
sections.body:
The [published study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07500-2) reports 9.8% attrition in the Airfare and IT divisions during the preceding six months. This is a division-level aggregate; the downloadable data does not supply an individual departure history or the earlier denominator. It provides historical context, while policy impact compares the two groups during the same later period.

No change predicts 9.8% attrition. The [earlier Ctrip study](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qju032) found about a 50% relative reduction with 4 home days a week among volunteer call-center staff. The simple two-day calculation assumes a proportional benefit: 9.8% × (1 − 50% × 2/4) = 7.35%. Scaling between different jobs, periods and schedules is an assumption. No after-policy outcomes enter either calculation. The simulation still uses its existing external turnover assumptions; the historical rate has not been used to refit those predictions.

sections.heading: What the prediction got right
sections.body:
Attrition: prediction -2.39 points (90% interval -5.16 to -0.20), experiment -2.40. Work satisfaction: prediction +0.37, experiment +0.35. Work-life balance: prediction +0.45, experiment +0.54. Performance grade: prediction +0.02, experiment -0.06 (experiment 95% CI -0.14 to +0.03; the prediction sits inside it). Take-up: prediction 55% of eligible days, experiment 52%.

The no-change prediction assumes zero policy impact. The simple two-day calculation predicts -2.45 percentage points, with an error of 0.05 points. This comparison applies only to overall attrition.

sections.heading: Where effects concentrate
sections.body:
Managers versus non-managers. Non-managers: prediction -2.8 points, experiment -3.3. Managers: prediction -1.1, experiment +0.2. The model produces this split from two independent facts: managers have lower baseline quit rates (older, longer tenure, management multiplier) and schedule-control gains are smaller where baseline autonomy is already high.

Commute. Employees with a two-way commute over 90 minutes: prediction -3.2 points, experiment -3.1; up to 90 minutes: prediction -1.8, experiment -2.6. Long commuters both take up WFH more and gain more from each day at home.

Gender. Women: prediction -2.1 points, experiment -5.0; men: prediction -2.6, experiment -1.0. Group differences arise from observed employee information from before the policy. Gender is excluded from behavior, commute imputation and synthetic role assignment.

sections.heading: What the policy variants show
sections.body:
Run on the same workforce with the same priors (20 matching simulation runs; attrition estimated by summing weekly hazards while employees remain at risk):

- The experiment as run: 8.8% office-only, 6.2% offered hybrid work, 7.5% overall.
- Hybrid for all: 6.1% company-wide, satisfaction 7.78, take-up 53%.
Trip.com extended hybrid work to the whole company after the experiment; the 'hybrid for all' row is the simulation's prediction of that decision.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body:
- Digital twins from real people: every simulated employee carries the real pretreatment covariate vector of one experiment employee, so the workforce has the experiment's exact joint distribution of commute, children, tenure, gender, education and role.
- O*NET-bound activities: 3 roles bound to O*NET-SOC occupations, 21 activities mapped to 35 detailed work activities, performed hour by hour and recorded in the run trace.
- Latent states: commute burden, work-life balance, job satisfaction and attachment evolve weekly from the policy exposure each person actually experiences, with weak sentiment spillover inside teams.
- Swappable policies: every WFH take-up and every stay-or-quit choice goes through a seat policy that picks among options the simulation supplies; a seat can be a transparent rule or a language model, by configuration.
- Digital twins with a trait layer: each employee carries fixed traits computed once per run (baseline satisfaction, baseline quit hazard, a WFH-preference trait that drives both how often they take a WFH day and how much each day is worth to them), a text profile built from those traits, and weekly latent states with inertia. The same twin feeds every seat policy, rule or language model.
- Team comparison: employees who are not offered WFH while their teammates are lose satisfaction in proportion to the share of teammates offered; arms were assigned within teams by birthday, so the comparison was salient.
- Independent priors: 34 behavioral parameters, each with a central value, a range and a cited source (the 2015 Ctrip full-time WFH experiment, turnover and commuting meta-analyses, the Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes, willingness-to-pay studies of flexible work, peer-comparison studies, industry turnover rates). The simulation reads neither arm's experiment outcomes. The inherited prior specification has been compared with this experiment before, so the results are retrospective, not a prospective validation.

sections.heading: Exploratory alternative: Employee AI assistant
sections.body:
Add an AI assistant for customer replies, notifications, requirements analysis, and operations analysis under the original hybrid-work policy. Estimate the effort released for other work after human review and correction. The comparison keeps the same employees, work schedule, and work-from-home offer. This is an exploratory application to the historical workforce, not an AI policy that Trip.com tested in this dataset.


5 matched simulation comparisons. No observed AI outcome is available.

| Outcome | Current policy | AI alternative | Difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Human effort for the work performed | 1573830.00 hours | 1539012.38 hours | -34817.62 hours |
| Hours released per employee over six months | 0.00 hours | 21.60 hours | +21.60 hours |
| Share of staff time released for other work | 0.00 % | 2.21 % | +2.21 pp |

All five settings below are editable scenario assumptions, not estimates fitted to Trip.com outcomes.
Coverage 60%; time saved before review 40%; review effort 15%; correction rate 10%; correction effort 100% of the task's ordinary effort.

Task shares are authored in the role definitions; hours are modeled from schedules and active employees, not measured time sheets. Released effort is capacity for other work, not cash savings or additional output. No link from AI assistance to satisfaction, resignations, or performance grades is assumed: unchanged values on those outcomes reflect this scope. Correction effort is included; residual errors and AI training and operating costs are not estimated.


[Noy & Zhang (2023): AI assistance on professional writing tasks](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adh2586). Motivates a task-time assumption; does not identify effects on these employees. [Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond (2025): AI assistance in customer support](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjae044). Evidence from a different employer; effects varied by experience. No retention effect is transferred.

quit_rate_semiannual.source: Baseline voluntary quit rate over ~24 weeks for Chinese white-collar/tech staff: annual voluntary turnover 15-20% (Aon Hewitt and Mercer China turnover surveys 2019-2021; internet sector above the all-industry mean), i.e. 7-10% per half year.

tenure_slope.source: Quit hazard declines with tenure: roughly 5-10% lower per additional year beyond the first (Farber 1994 'The analysis of interfirm worker mobility', JOLE; job-matching models).

manager_hazard_mult.source: Voluntary turnover at management level is about half to two thirds of the staff level (SHRM Human Capital Benchmarking; Mercer turnover surveys).

wfh_full_quit_hr.source: Ctrip 2015 full-time WFH experiment: attrition fell by about 50% among WFH employees over nine months (Bloom, Liang, Roberts & Ying, QJE 2015, doi:10.7910/DVN/PZQOB1). Hazard ratio for five-day WFH; the three channels below (satisfaction, commute, direct flexibility) sum to this total.

beta_sat.source: Job satisfaction to turnover meta-analyses: rho = -0.19 to -0.28 (Griffeth, Hom & Gaertner 2000; Rubenstein et al. 2018), i.e. a hazard ratio of about 0.65 per SD of satisfaction; with SD ~2 points on a 0-10 scale this is 0.21 log-hazard per point.

beta_commute.source: Longer commutes raise quit intention and job switching: about 10-20% higher per extra hour of daily commuting (van Ommeren & Gutierrez-i-Puigarnau 2011, Regional Science and Urban Economics; Chatterjee et al. 2020 Transport Reviews). Per two-way commute hour per working day.

d_sat_full.source: Full-time WFH raised work-attitude survey scores significantly in the 2015 Ctrip trial (Bloom et al. 2015, Table on attitudes); telecommuting-job satisfaction meta-analysis r ~ 0.1 (Gajendran & Harrison 2007, JAP). Taken as ~0.3 SD = 0.6 points on 0-10.

d_wlb_full.source: Telecommuting reduces work-family conflict by d ~ 0.3-0.45 (Gajendran & Harrison 2007; Allen, Golden & Shockley 2015, Psychological Science in the Public Interest), plus ~1.5 commute hours saved per WFH day (SWAA, Barrero, Bloom & Davis 2021).

hybrid_value_share_2d.source: Amenity value of two WFH days relative to five. Workers' desired WFH is ~2.3-2.5 days a week and a majority prefer hybrid to fully remote (Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes, Barrero, Bloom & Davis 2021 'Why working from home will stick'); over half of the full-time WFH employees in the 2015 Ctrip experiment chose to return to the office when it ended, citing isolation (Bloom, Liang, Roberts & Ying 2015), so five days carry disamenities that two do not. v1 used 0.7 [0.5, 0.9].

pref_value_slope.source: Willingness to pay for the option to work from home is highly dispersed across workers: about 8% of wages on average with a large mass near zero and a long right tail (Mas & Pallais 2017, AER 'Valuing alternative work arrangements'; Maestas, Mullen, Powell, von Wachter & Wenger 2023, AER 'The value of working conditions in the United States'). Log-scale slope of the per-day benefit on the standardized WFH-preference trait, the same trait that drives take-up (Roy 1951 selection on gains). Normalised so that the upper half of the preference distribution, the population that volunteered in the 2015 Ctrip experiment (503 of 996 eligible), has mean value 1, because the 2015 attrition hazard ratio was measured on that population.

relative_deprivation_k.source: Employees denied an amenity that their teammates receive compare themselves with those peers: disclosing peers' higher pay lowered job satisfaction and raised job-search intentions among below-median earners (Card, Mas, Moretti & Saez 2012, AER 'Inequality at work'); equity theory (Adams 1965). Points of job satisfaction (0-10) lost by an employee not offered WFH when all teammates are offered it, scaled by the share of teammates offered. Arms were assigned within teams by birthday parity, so the comparison was salient every Wednesday and Friday.

option_value_share.source: Workers value the option of schedule flexibility even when they rarely use it: willingness to pay is elicited for the option to work from home (Mas & Pallais 2017, AER 'Valuing alternative work arrangements'), and SWAA respondents using two WFH days value the arrangement at about 8% of pay (Barrero, Bloom & Davis 2021). Share of the realised-WFH benefit accruing to eligible employees on days they come in. v1-v2 used 0.25 [0, 0.5].

manager_effect_share.source: Schedule-control interventions help most where baseline control is low (Kelly, Moen et al. 2014 STAR trial, American Sociological Review); managers already hold more autonomy and coordination duties, so their benefit is attenuated.

children_value_boost.source: Parents of young children value WFH more and report larger time savings (SWAA, Barrero, Bloom & Davis 2021). Multiplicative uplift on the benefit for employees with children.

takeup_base.source: About half of eligible employees volunteered for WFH in the 2015 Ctrip trial (503 of 996; Bloom et al. 2015); ~55-60% of workers want two or more WFH days (SWAA 2021). Share of eligible WFH days taken by the average eligible employee.

b_takeup_commute.source: Commute time is the strongest predictor of the desire to WFH (SWAA, Barrero, Bloom & Davis 2021). Logit slope per one-way commute hour.

b_takeup_children.source: Parents want more WFH days (SWAA 2021). Logit shift.

b_takeup_volunteer.source: Revealed preference: employees who volunteered for the trial before the lottery asked for WFH. Logit shift.

takeup_sd.source: Authored: between-person heterogeneity in WFH preference on the logit scale (wide, so take-up spans 0.2-0.8 across people).

adjust_rate.source: Authored: attitudes adjust to a new arrangement within one to two months (hedonic adaptation literature, e.g. Luhmann et al. 2012). Weekly adjustment fraction.

contagion_k.source: Weak within-team sentiment spillover (Barsade 2002 emotional contagion; Felps et al. 2009 turnover contagion, AMJ). Weekly pull toward the team mean.

beta_attach.source: Affective organisational commitment predicts voluntary turnover (rho = -0.17 with turnover, -0.56 with turnover intention; Meyer, Stanley, Herscovitch & Topolnytsky 2002, Journal of Vocational Behavior), about OR 0.55 per SD of commitment. Attachment here has SD ~0.15 on its 0-1 scale, so the full meta-analytic value is ~3 log-hazard per unit; set to one third of that (1.0) because the instantaneous satisfaction, commute and amenity channels already carry part of the commitment effect. Log-hazard per unit change of attachment from its start-of-run value.

attach_rate.source: Authored: attachment is a slow stock of accumulated satisfaction and flexibility.

sat_anchor.source: Approximate mean job satisfaction of urban white-collar workers in China on a 0-10 scale (CGSS/CFPS job-satisfaction items average ~3.6-3.8 on five points). The ITT contrasts do not depend on the anchor.

sat_sd.source: Typical between-person SD of 0-10 satisfaction items (1.5-2.0; e.g. ESS, SWAA).

wlb_anchor.source: Authored: work-life balance rated slightly below job satisfaction for long-commute office workers.

survey_noise_sd.source: Single-item satisfaction test-retest reliability ~0.7 implies measurement noise of ~0.8 points (Wanous, Reichers & Hudy 1997).

perf_rho.source: Performance-rating stability over one year ~0.5-0.6 (Sturman, Cheramie & Cashen 2005, JAP meta-analysis).

d_perf_full.source: Centred near zero: the 2015 call-centre trial found output up 13% but review/promotion effects ambiguous; hybrid field evidence outside this trial (Choudhury et al. 2024, SMJ) finds no performance loss. Grade points per unit exposure.

promo_rate_semiannual.source: Annual promotion rates of 10-15% in large firms (Mercer, Baker-Gibbs-Holmstrom style personnel data), i.e. 5-8% per half year.

promo_hr_full.source: Full-time WFH roughly halved promotion conditional on performance in the 2015 Ctrip trial; hybrid keeps in-office visibility, so the prior is attenuated toward one.

promo_grade_slope.source: Authored: promotion odds rise with the review grade.

/report.title: Hybrid work at Trip.com: simulation prediction and actual outcome
/report.subtitle: 1612 employees, six months, two WFH days a week offered to half of them. Simulation from pretreatment inputs and assumptions from earlier research; compared with Bloom, Han & Liang (Nature 2024).
takeaways: The simulation predicts a 2.39 percentage-point reduction in six-month attrition from offering two home days a week. The actual reduction was 2.40 points, comparing the hybrid and office-only groups.

Six-month attrition: the simulation predicts 8.6% for office-only employees and 6.3% for employees offered hybrid work. Actual outcomes were 7.2% and 4.8%, respectively. Both simulated rates are too high.
The simulation predicts work satisfaction increasing by +0.37 points on the 0-10 scale; the actual increase was +0.35. Work-life balance: simulation prediction +0.45, actual outcome +0.54.
The retention gain concentrates among non-managers: prediction -2.8 points for non-managers and -1.1 for managers; the experiment measured -3.3 and +0.2.
For performance grades, the simulation predicts a change of +0.02 points; the actual change was -0.06. Both estimates are small.
Simulated employees used 55% of their eligible WFH days; the experiment recorded 52%.

This is a retrospective comparison with published outcomes. Earlier model choices had already been compared with those results; the close overall impact does not establish accuracy on new companies or policies.
Extending the offer to everyone takes company-wide six-month attrition from 7.5% (the experiment as run, simulated) to 6.1%, about 24 fewer resignations among 1612 employees.

sections.heading: What was simulated
sections.body: 1612 employees of Trip.com's Airfare and IT divisions, rebuilt one by one from the experiment's real pretreatment data (age, gender, tenure, graduate degree, children, commute time, volunteer status, prior performance grade, manager flag) and assigned to the arms exactly as the birthday lottery did: 820 / 792 office-only / offered hybrid work. Each employee works an hourly schedule from 9 Aug 2021 to 23 Jan 2022, performing O*NET-bound activities of their role, commuting on office days and, in the group offered hybrid work, deciding every Wednesday and Friday whether to work from home. Latent commute burden, work-life balance, job satisfaction and attachment update weekly; a weekly quit hazard turns those states into resignations. The endline survey (21 Jan 2022) and the 2021H2 performance review are simulated as the company recorded them. The prediction was run over 50 seeds with every behavioral parameter drawn from its prior range, so the intervals reflect prior uncertainty and simulated outcome variation. This is a retrospective evaluation, not an untouched prospective test.

sections.heading: Before the policy and the other predictions
sections.body:
The [published study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07500-2) reports 9.8% attrition in the Airfare and IT divisions during the preceding six months. This is a division-level aggregate; the downloadable data does not supply an individual departure history or the earlier denominator. It provides historical context, while policy impact compares the two groups during the same later period.

No change predicts 9.8% attrition. The [earlier Ctrip study](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qju032) found about a 50% relative reduction with 4 home days a week among volunteer call-center staff. The simple two-day calculation assumes a proportional benefit: 9.8% × (1 − 50% × 2/4) = 7.35%. Scaling between different jobs, periods and schedules is an assumption. No after-policy outcomes enter either calculation. The simulation still uses its existing external turnover assumptions; the historical rate has not been used to refit those predictions.

sections.heading: What the prediction got right
sections.body:
Attrition: prediction -2.39 points (90% interval -5.16 to -0.20), experiment -2.40. Work satisfaction: prediction +0.37, experiment +0.35. Work-life balance: prediction +0.45, experiment +0.54. Performance grade: prediction +0.02, experiment -0.06 (experiment 95% CI -0.14 to +0.03; the prediction sits inside it). Take-up: prediction 55% of eligible days, experiment 52%.

The no-change prediction assumes zero policy impact. The simple two-day calculation predicts -2.45 percentage points, with an error of 0.05 points. This comparison applies only to overall attrition.

sections.heading: Where effects concentrate
sections.body:
Managers versus non-managers. Non-managers: prediction -2.8 points, experiment -3.3. Managers: prediction -1.1, experiment +0.2. The model produces this split from two independent facts: managers have lower baseline quit rates (older, longer tenure, management multiplier) and schedule-control gains are smaller where baseline autonomy is already high.

Commute. Employees with a two-way commute over 90 minutes: prediction -3.2 points, experiment -3.1; up to 90 minutes: prediction -1.8, experiment -2.6. Long commuters both take up WFH more and gain more from each day at home.

Gender. Women: prediction -2.1 points, experiment -5.0; men: prediction -2.6, experiment -1.0. Group differences arise from observed employee information from before the policy. Gender is excluded from behavior, commute imputation and synthetic role assignment.

sections.heading: What the policy variants show
sections.body:
Run on the same workforce with the same priors (20 matching simulation runs; attrition estimated by summing weekly hazards while employees remain at risk):

- The experiment as run: 8.8% office-only, 6.2% offered hybrid work, 7.5% overall.
- Hybrid for all: 6.1% company-wide, satisfaction 7.78, take-up 53%.
Trip.com extended hybrid work to the whole company after the experiment; the 'hybrid for all' row is the simulation's prediction of that decision.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body:
- Digital twins from real people: every simulated employee carries the real pretreatment covariate vector of one experiment employee, so the workforce has the experiment's exact joint distribution of commute, children, tenure, gender, education and role.
- O*NET-bound activities: 3 roles bound to O*NET-SOC occupations, 21 activities mapped to 35 detailed work activities, performed hour by hour and recorded in the run trace.
- Latent states: commute burden, work-life balance, job satisfaction and attachment evolve weekly from the policy exposure each person actually experiences, with weak sentiment spillover inside teams.
- Swappable policies: every WFH take-up and every stay-or-quit choice goes through a seat policy that picks among options the simulation supplies; a seat can be a transparent rule or a language model, by configuration.
- Digital twins with a trait layer: each employee carries fixed traits computed once per run (baseline satisfaction, baseline quit hazard, a WFH-preference trait that drives both how often they take a WFH day and how much each day is worth to them), a text profile built from those traits, and weekly latent states with inertia. The same twin feeds every seat policy, rule or language model.
- Team comparison: employees who are not offered WFH while their teammates are lose satisfaction in proportion to the share of teammates offered; arms were assigned within teams by birthday, so the comparison was salient.
- Independent priors: 34 behavioral parameters, each with a central value, a range and a cited source (the 2015 Ctrip full-time WFH experiment, turnover and commuting meta-analyses, the Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes, willingness-to-pay studies of flexible work, peer-comparison studies, industry turnover rates). The simulation reads neither arm's experiment outcomes. The inherited prior specification has been compared with this experiment before, so the results are retrospective, not a prospective validation.

sections.heading: Exploratory alternative: Employee AI assistant
sections.body:
Add an AI assistant for customer replies, notifications, requirements analysis, and operations analysis under the original hybrid-work policy. Estimate the effort released for other work after human review and correction. The comparison keeps the same employees, work schedule, and work-from-home offer. This is an exploratory application to the historical workforce, not an AI policy that Trip.com tested in this dataset.


5 matched simulation comparisons. No observed AI outcome is available.

| Outcome | Current policy | AI alternative | Difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Human effort for the work performed | 1573830.00 hours | 1539012.38 hours | -34817.62 hours |
| Hours released per employee over six months | 0.00 hours | 21.60 hours | +21.60 hours |
| Share of staff time released for other work | 0.00 % | 2.21 % | +2.21 pp |

All five settings below are editable scenario assumptions, not estimates fitted to Trip.com outcomes.
Coverage 60%; time saved before review 40%; review effort 15%; correction rate 10%; correction effort 100% of the task's ordinary effort.

Task shares are authored in the role definitions; hours are modeled from schedules and active employees, not measured time sheets. Released effort is capacity for other work, not cash savings or additional output. No link from AI assistance to satisfaction, resignations, or performance grades is assumed: unchanged values on those outcomes reflect this scope. Correction effort is included; residual errors and AI training and operating costs are not estimated.


[Noy & Zhang (2023): AI assistance on professional writing tasks](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adh2586). Motivates a task-time assumption; does not identify effects on these employees. [Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond (2025): AI assistance in customer support](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjae044). Evidence from a different employer; effects varied by experience. No retention effect is transferred.
